# Architecture (/docs/architecture)

Five layers, each one only there because without it a specific thing fails. The diagram is the fast way to understand the rig; the table below is the "why".

<Mermaid chart="flowchart TB\n  subgraph host[\"Host (Linux Mint)\"]\n      M[mitmdump :18080<br/>mitm/dump.py]\n      T[adb reverse tcp:18080]\n      F[frida CLI 17.27.5]\n      CDP[cdp / session<br/>CDP :9222]\n      R[replay / recon / snap]\n  end\n\n  subgraph emu[\"pentest16 — Android 16 x86_64\"]\n      subgraph zyg[\"Zygote (Zygisk Next)\"]\n          TS[TrickyStore<br/>attestation spoof]\n          PIF[PlayIntegrityFix 4.9]\n          HMA[HMA-OSS<br/>app list filter]\n      end\n      MAG[Magisk 31.1 + su]\n      CF[Cert-Fixer<br/>CA bind-mount]\n      FS[frida-server as 'hluda'<br/>127.0.0.1:27042]\n      APP[Target app<br/>+ WebView]\n  end\n\n  F -->|frida protocol| FS\n  FS --> APP\n  M --- T --- APP\n  M -.->|flows| R\n  CF -.->|trust| APP\n  TS -.->|keystore| APP\n  MAG --> FS\n  MAG --> zyg\n  CDP -->|websocket| APP\n  R -->|replay| M" />

## The layers, in dependency order [#the-layers-in-dependency-order]

### 1. Emulator [#1-emulator]

`pentest16` is a **Play Store** (`google_apis_playstore`) system image for API 36, x86_64, pixel_7 profile, 6 GB RAM, 16 GB data partition. Play Store matters: several attestation-ish code paths check for GMS presence and behave differently without it.

It runs with KVM acceleration (`/dev/kvm`, user in `kvm` group), 4 vCPUs, and GPU on. Boot from cold is ~90 s; from a snapshot, ~25 s.

### 2. Root — rootAVD + Magisk [#2-root--rootavd--magisk]

`rootAVD` patches `ramdisk.img` of the **system image** (not the AVD) with Magisk, then the Magisk app does a second "additional setup" pass on first boot. Result: `su` works, `context=u:r:magisk:s0`.

Magisk 31.1 specifics that bite:

- Built-in Zygisk must be **off** (`magisk --sqlite "replace into settings (key,value) values('zygisk',0)"`) because **Zygisk Next** owns injection.
- Magisk's denylist is **empty** by design here. Adding an app would strip our modules (TrickyStore, PIF) from exactly the app that needs them.
- `magisk --denylist rm <pkg> <process>` (two args) **segfaults the daemon**. Use one argument.

### 3. Zygisk modules [#3-zygisk-modules]

| Module | id | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Zygisk Next 1.5.3 | `zygisksu` | The injector. `zygiskd` CLI controls policy, memory type, module list. |
| TrickyStore 1.4.1 | `tricky_store` | Replaces the keystore's attestation certificate chain for packages in `target.txt` using `keybox.xml`. |
| PlayIntegrityFix 4.9 | `playintegrityfix` | Tries to satisfy Play Integrity. On an emulator: **NO_INTEGRITY**, permanently. |
| HMA-OSS (Vector-flavoured) | `hma_oss_zygisk` | Hides other installed packages from a target app (root/emulator detector enumeration). |
| Cert-Fixer 1.1 | `cert-fixer` | Bind-mounts user CAs into `/apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts` at `post-fs-data`, so **GMS and Play Store** trust mitmproxy too. |
| fsrv (ours) | `fsrv` | Renames and autostarts `frida-server` as `/data/adb/fsrv/hluda`, loopback only. |

Zygisk Next's memory type is set to **anonymous** so module libs never appear in `/proc/<pid>/maps` as files.

### 4. Interception [#4-interception]

<Mermaid chart="sequenceDiagram\n  participant App\n  participant Proxy as mitmdump :18080\n  participant Up as upstream\n  App->>Proxy: HTTP/2 CONNECT (adb reverse tunnel)\n  Proxy->>Up: TLS to real server\n  Note over Proxy: dump.py writes /tmp/mtflows/<HHMMSS>_<host>_<path>.txt\n  Proxy-->>App: TLS with mitmproxy CA\n  Note over App: CA trusted because Cert-Fixer mounted it into conscrypt" />

Two details make this painless:

- **`adb reverse`** (device → host), not a proxy on the LAN, so no `http_proxy` is needed for pinned apps. `adb reverse` dies on every reboot; `nettap on` restores it.
- **Cert-Fixer** mounts the CA at boot for the *whole system*, which is why Play Store and GMS traffic decrypts instead of failing with `does not trust the proxy's certificate`.

### 5. Host tooling [#5-host-tooling]

`pentestctl` (health), `nettap` (proxy+tunnel+addon), `fspawn` (spawn under Frida with a profile), `fdp`/`cdp` (WebView DevTools), `session` (harvest cookies+storage), `replay` (re-issue requests), `recon` (static APK), `snap` (AVD snapshots), `uitap` (UI automation), `asu` (run root snippets).

## What fails if you remove a layer [#what-fails-if-you-remove-a-layer]

| Remove | Symptom |
|---|---|
| Cert-Fixer | Chrome/WebView still decrypts (user CA), but **Play Store and GMS** throw TLS handshake errors. |
| TrickyStore `target.txt` entry | App gets the emulator's fake AOSP chain → server rejects with an attestation error. |
| Valid keybox | Chain becomes the bundled **software** AOSP keybox (expired intermediate) → server rejects. |
| `zygiskd enforce-denylist` off | Nothing breaks; denylist simply stops being honoured. |
| `adb reverse` | App talks to a dead proxy: spinner forever, zero flows. This is the #1 "it broke overnight" cause. |
| Zygisk Next | No TrickyStore, no PIF, no HMA — attestation spoof and hiding both vanish. |

## Design decisions worth knowing [#design-decisions-worth-knowing]

- **Play Store image over AOSP** — closer to a real device for attestation checks; the cost is a heavier boot and GMS noise in every capture (filtered by `IGNORE` in `dump.py`).
- **Denylist policy `default`, not `whitelist`** — whitelist mode injects only for listed packages, but WebView renderer sandbox processes (`…:sandboxed_process0`, isolated uid) never match the package name, so every page load failed with `net_error -202`. Tried it, reverted it; see [Root hiding](/docs/stealth#whitelist-trap).
- **frida-server, not gadget** — gadget needs per-APK patching and re-signing, which changes the APK signature (and some servers check it). Server-side injection leaves the APK untouched.
- **Loopback-only frida** — `LISTEN=127.0.0.1:27042` + `adb` forwarding. Nothing on the LAN can reach the agent, and no `frida-server` string appears in a listening-socket scan.

# Attestation & keyboxes (/docs/attestation)

This is the part that usually makes people give up on emulator-based testing. A modern app asks the **Android keystore** to generate a key with a server-chosen challenge, and the keystore returns a certificate chain signed by Google's servers describing the device. The app ships that chain to its backend, which decides whether to let you in.

On an emulator that chain says *"Droid Unregistered Device CA, Google Test LLC"* — an obvious emulator. On a real phone it says *"hardware-backed, verified boot green, your device"*. Even with a software keybox the chain is signed by an **expired** AOSP intermediate. Both get rejected.

<Mermaid chart="sequenceDiagram\n  participant App\n  participant KS as Android Keystore\n  participant TS as TrickyStore (Zygisk)\n  participant Srv as Backend\n  App->>KS: generateKey(alias, attestationChallenge)\n  KS->>TS: real chain (or AOSP fake chain)\n  TS-->>App: substituted chain from keybox.xml\n  App->>Srv: POST /login { attestation: { chain: [...] } }\n  Srv->>Srv: verify chain against Google roots + revocation list\n  Srv-->>App: 2000 (accepted) or 4202 (ATTESTATION_UNSUPPORTED)" />

## TrickyStore [#trickystore]

- Module id `tricky_store`, manager UI in `com.example.target`-style apps is not needed — it is driven by two files.
- `target.txt` — one package per line: **only these apps** get spoofed chains.
- `keybox.xml` — the replacement chain material (EC and/or RSA), plus the private keys that let the keystore actually sign with it.
- Reads `tee_status`; on an emulator `teeBroken=true` is expected.

```bash
adb shell su -c 'cat /data/adb/tricky_store/target.txt'
adb shell su -c 'grep -o "DeviceID=\"[^\"]*\"" /data/adb/tricky_store/keybox.xml'
```

<Callout type="info" title="DeviceID is cosmetic — do not read identity into it">
The `DeviceID` attribute is just a label the upstream keybox author typed. For the public
`RED-TEAM-KEYBOX` source it is literally a Telegram advert
(`DeviceID="RKP keybox. Join my group: t.me/redteamchannell"`). TrickyStore never uses it and the
server validates the **chain**, not the label — so it is normal for it to look like spam and to
change on every `keybox-refresh`. `pentestctl status` prints it tagged *(cosmetic upstream label)*.
</Callout>

<Callout type="warn" title="Forgetting target.txt looks like a broken keybox">
Before adding the package, the app still receives the emulator's own fake chain. The server says *"this device could not be verified"* and you blame the keybox. Add the package, force-stop the app, relaunch — no reboot required.
</Callout>

## Keybox lifecycle [#keybox-lifecycle]

A usable keybox must satisfy **all** of:

1. Chain signatures verify up to a known root.
2. Nothing in the chain is **expired**.
3. The serial numbers are **not on Google's revocation list** (`https://android.googleapis.com/attestation/status`).
4. It is a **hardware/RKP** chain — the server can tell software chains apart, and they are rejected by anything modern.

Check all four before installing:

```bash
kbcheck.py --summary /tmp/kb.xml
# SUMMARY device=<cosmetic upstream label> alg=ecdsa len=4 root=None sig=ok leaf_not_after=2026-12-04 revoked=- expired=-
kbcheck.py --strict /tmp/kb.xml      # exit 1 unless every check passes
```

`root=None` is normal: the bundled root bundle (`tools/keybox-res/`) predates the RKP root (`CN=Key Attestation CA1`), so the root *pin* cannot be matched — signatures and revocation still validate, and the server is the real judge.

### The one that works right now [#the-one-that-works-right-now]

```bash
setup-keybox.sh                       # fetch from upstream, validate, install, back up the old one
keybox-refresh                        # same thing, but only if it is actually needed
pentestctl status | grep keybox
#   --   keybox DeviceID="RKP keybox. Join my group: t.me/redteamchannell" (cosmetic upstream label, not an identity — the chain is what matters)
#   ok   keybox leaf valid until 2026-12-04 (8d left)
```

Source: `redteam-git/RED-TEAM-KEYBOX` publishes a base64 blob at `…/main/conf` (refreshed every 4 h upstream). `setup-keybox.sh --file <xml>` installs a local file; `--check` validates only.

### Keeping it alive: `keybox-refresh` [#keeping-it-alive-keybox-refresh]

Keyboxes die quietly — the leaf expires and the server starts answering `4202` again with no other symptom. `keybox-refresh` is the boring fix:

```bash
keybox-refresh                 # refresh only if < 7 days left, revoked, or already expired
keybox-refresh --force         # refresh now, e.g. when the target starts refusing you
keybox-refresh --min-days 20   # keep a wider safety margin
keybox-refresh --dry-run       # validate the device keybox and print what it would do
```

How it behaves:

1. Reads the device keybox, runs `kbcheck.py --summary` (`device=… leaf_not_after=… sig=… revoked=…`).
2. Stays put unless the keybox is close to expiry or already dead.
3. Tries sources in order — `redteam`, then `yuri` — accepting only payloads that `kbcheck.py --strict` accepts (signatures, chain, expiry, of the revocation list).
4. Backs up the old keybox as `keybox.xml.bak_<ts>` and force-stops `com.example.target`, `com.android.vending`, `com.google.android.gms` so they re-open the keystore.
5. Appends to `~/.mobsec/keybox.log`.

It runs automatically through a **systemd user timer** (`mobsec-keybox.timer`: 10 min after boot, then daily with a randomised delay, `Persistent=true`):

```bash
systemctl --user list-timers | grep mobsec
systemctl --user start mobsec-keybox.service    # run it now
journalctl --user -u mobsec-keybox.service -n 20
```

The current leaf expires **2026-12-04**; `pentestctl status` prints the remaining days on every run, so the timer is a safety net and not the primary signal.

### Anatomy of a rejected keybox (real example) [#anatomy-of-a-rejected-keybox-real-example]

The well-known Yurikey keybox had a perfect hardware chain — and its leaf serial `bb0d83fa2a47a1ae54c8c359778aaf35` was on Google's revocation list (2222 entries). Everything looked right in the UI, and the server still said no. Always check revocation, not just expiry.

## What the server actually validates [#what-the-server-actually-validates]

From the target app's behaviour, in order of strictness:

1. Chain parses and every signature verifies.
2. Leaf public key matches the challenge-signed data.
3. Chain contains Google's RKP attestation extension (hardware root of trust).
4. No serial is revoked, nothing expired.
5. Sometimes: `verifiedBootState` = green, `deviceLocked` = true, `osVersion` sane.

TrickyStore supplies 1–5 for keystore users, but the **revocation list** is checked server-side and cannot be spoofed locally. That is why a revoked keybox is worthless even though the UI shows a beautiful chain.

## Verifying on-device [#verifying-on-device]

Install **KeyAttestation** (`io.github.vvb2060.keyattestation`, in `apks/`) and generate a key:

- ✅ expected: `CN=App Attest Key` issued by `O=TEE,CN=<32 hex>`, "Bootloader is locked", manufacturer from the keybox, ~32 certs issued in the last 30 days.
- ⚠️ expected on this rig: banner *"Unknown root certificate — root is not a known trusted CA"*. Its local root pool does not contain the RKP root; the target server's does. Not a failure.
- ❌ if you see `CN=Android Keystore Software Attestation Intermediate`: `target.txt` is missing the package, or `keybox.xml` is the bundled software one.

## Play Integrity is a different problem [#play-integrity-is-a-different-problem]

Play Integrity's `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY` cannot be faked on an emulator; measured here as **UNEVALUATED** (Google declines to grade an emulator with no account) before and after PlayIntegrityFix. This rig does not solve PI, and does not need to for apps that use raw key attestation. The mechanics, the `integrity` tool and the escape routes are on the [Play Integrity](/docs/integrity) page.

<Callout type="info" title="x86_64 gotcha">
`PlayIntegrityFork` v19 ships only arm64/armv7 `zygisk` libs, so on this x86_64 image it silently never loads (`zygiskd status` stops listing `playintegrityfix`). The installed module is `PlayIntegrityFix_v4.9-inject-s.zip`, which does ship x86_64. v19 is parked in `modules/archive/`.
</Callout>

# Pentest checklist (mapped to this rig) (/docs/checklist)

This is the HackTricks/OWASP-MASTG Android checklist, rewritten as *"which command in this rig does that, and where does it stop working"*. Use it so you do not reinvent steps — and so you do not claim coverage the emulator cannot give you.

Legend: **✔** a command does it · **~** partial, read the note · **✘** impossible or pointless here.

## 1. Before you install anything (static) [#1-before-you-install-anything-static]

| Check | Command | |
|---|---|---|
| What is it, who signed it, which SDKs | `recon app.apk` | ✔ |
| Obfuscation / packer / anti-VM hints | `recon` → Packers section (`apkid`) | ✔ |
| `APKiD` says `anti_vm` / `anti_debug` | verify by hand in jadx — it fires on Google/Firebase/Material library code | ~ |
| Secrets, API keys, endpoints in DEX/resources | `recon --deep`, then `apkleaks` section | ✔ |
| Rule-based SAST (Weak crypto, WebView, backup flags…) | `recon` → `mobsfscan` | ✔ |
| Manifest triage: exported components, deep links, `allowBackup`, `dataExtractionRules`, `networkSecurityConfig`, `usesCleartextTraffic`, `debuggable` | `recon` (summary) + `entry` (attack sheet) | ✔ |
| App Links / `assetlinks.json` | `entry` → "App links on this device" | ✔ |
| Native libs + CVEs | `apkanalyzer apk summary`, `unzip -l`; CVE mapping by hand | ~ |
| Cross-platform framework (Flutter/RN/Tauri/Cordova) | `find lib/ -name '*.so'`; Tauri = `libapp_lib.so` + remote web UI | ✔ |
| Decompile for source review | `jadx-gui app.apk` (or `apktool d`) | ✔ |
| Sideloaded/store differences | compare APKs from Play vs vendor — Play App Signing changes the signing key | ~ |

## 2. Install and get it running [#2-install-and-get-it-running]

| Check | Command | |
|---|---|---|
| Get past root/emulator detection | `fspawn <pkg> intercept` (HTTP Toolkit set: root detection off, pinning off, proxy overridden) | ✔ |
| Get past key attestation | `setup-keybox.sh` / `keybox-refresh`, target listed in `/data/adb/tricky_store/target.txt` | ✔ |
| Get past Play Integrity | see [Play Integrity](/docs/integrity) — not passable on an emulator | ✘ |
| Force the app to talk to you | `nettap on` (proxy + reverse + addon), then use the app | ✔ |
| Launch an exported activity/service/receiver | `entry <pkg> --run` | ✔ |
| See what it does with a URL | `entry <pkg> --only links` | ✔ |

## 3. Runtime: storage [#3-runtime-storage]

| Check | Command | |
|---|---|---|
| Private dir, sqlite, prefs, webview store | `pull-data <pkg>` (`--sql`, `--grep`) | ✔ |
| What is *actually* in the databases | `sqlite3 ~/.mobsec/data/<pkg>/…/foo.db .dump` | ✔ |
| Session/refresh tokens at rest | `pull-data --grep token` → then decrypt by hand if needed | ✔ |
| Keystore-backed keys | `fspawn <pkg> attest` (`20-keystore.js` dumps subject/issuer of generated chains) | ✔ |
| "Keystore is hardware-backed" claim | KeyAttestation app → see [Attestation](/docs/attestation) | ✔ |
| `adb backup` extraction | blocked on API 31+ unless the app opts in; use `pull-data` instead | ~ |
| External storage / shared prefs | `pull-data` also pulls `/sdcard/Android/data/<pkg>` | ✔ |

## 4. Runtime: network [#4-runtime-network]

| Check | Command | |
|---|---|---|
| Full request set, decrypted | `nettap on` + `flows` (files in `/tmp/mtflows`, index in `_index.jsonl`) | ✔ |
| Pinning | `fspawn <pkg> intercept` | ✔ |
| Proxy-unaware / native traffic | same profile (in-process proxy override) | ✔ |
| WebSocket / GraphQL over WS | flows capture the handshake; `cdp watch` shows app-side messages | ~ |
| Edit and re-send a request | `replay --grep PATH --patch 'field=value'` | ✔ |
| IDOR / authz testing | `snap list` → clone the AVD, log in as user B (`ANDROID_SERIAL`), replay user A's requests | ~ |
| MQTT/gRPC/QUIC/bluetooth | nothing here terminates those; check the app's protocol first | ✘ |

## 5. Runtime: WebView / hybrid apps [#5-runtime-webview--hybrid-apps]

| Check | Command | |
|---|---|---|
| DOM, localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies | `fdp` then `cdp eval 'location.href'` / `session harvest` | ✔ |
| Console + network of the web layer | `cdp watch 30` | ✔ |
| `addJavascriptInterface` bridges | `fspawn <pkg> web` shows console; grep the bundle for the bridge name | ~ |
| Client-side authz enforced in JS | read the bundle: `grep -o 'plugin:[^"]*' *.js` finds Tauri/Electron IPC commands | ✔ |
| Deep links into the web layer | `entry` + `cdp eval 'location.href="/route"'` | ✔ |

## 6. Runtime: components and injection [#6-runtime-components-and-injection]

| Check | Command | |
|---|---|---|
| Exported components reachable, permission NOT enforced | `entry <pkg> --run`, watch logcat | ✔ |
| Content provider data leak | `entry` provider lines (`content query --uri …`) — note `exported=false` + `grantUriPermissions=true` needs a grant | ~ |
| Task hijacking / StrandHogg | needs a real launcher and a second malicious app — out of scope for this rig | ✘ |
| Tapjacking / overlay attacks | needs overlay permissions and a real UI; emulator OK but no template here | ✘ |
| Dynamic instrumentation | `fspawn <pkg> trace\|attest\|web\|spy` | ✔ |
| Root/emulator checks firing | `fspawn <pkg> trace` → `30-rootcheck.js` prints each path/API queried | ✔ |

## 7. Server side (where the money usually is) [#7-server-side-where-the-money-usually-is]

| Check | Command | |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint inventory | `flows` index + `recon --deep` endpoints, diffed | ✔ |
| Authz: object ownership | `replay` with another user's ids | ✔ |
| Mass assignment / field injection | `replay --patch` | ✔ |
| Rate limits / lockout | `replay` in a loop, watch status codes | ✔ |
| MFA weaknesses | `session harvest` → inspect `/auth/session`-style endpoints for seeds/tokens | ✔ |
| Logout / session invalidation | `replay` the logout, then reuse the cookie | ✔ |

## 8. What this rig cannot tell you [#8-what-this-rig-cannot-tell-you]

- Anything hardware-backed that you did not spoof: sensors, Secure Element, StrongBox, real TEE behaviour.
- Play Integrity verdicts ([why](/docs/integrity)).
- Bluetooth, NFC, USB, SIM/telephony behaviour.
- OEM-specific bugs (the emulator is AOSP + Google image, no vendor blobs).
- Performance/timing side channels that depend on real CPU and memory pressure.
- Whether a leaked key matters — that is a server-side validation question, and the answer changes per target.

## Reporting habit [#reporting-habit]

For every finding, keep the evidence triple: **the flow file** (`/tmp/mtflows/…txt`), **the replay command** that reproduces it, and **the app state** (which `snap` image, which user, which Frida profile). `_index.jsonl` plus a one-line `replay` command is the cheapest possible repro packet.

# Captured flows & replay (/docs/flows)

Every interesting request on the device ends up as a file in `/tmp/mtflows` (change with `FLOWDIR`). Those files are the raw material for everything else: analysis, replay, fuzzing, evidence.

## Format [#format]

One file per flow, named `<HHMMSS>_<host>_<path>.txt`:

```text
POST https://crmbff.example.com/auth/mobile/login

--REQ HEADERS--
Headers[(b'content-type', b'application/json'), (b'cookie', b'mtpo.crm=…'), …]

--REQ BODY--
{"userName":"…","password":"…","attestation":{"chain":[ … ]}}

--RESP 200--
Headers[(b'content-type', b'application/json'), …]

--RESP BODY--
{"code":2000,"data":{…}}
```

Notes:

- The headers block is mitmproxy's `Headers` repr on **one line** — parse with `ast.literal_eval` after stripping the `Headers` prefix (that is what `replay` does).
- Bodies are truncated at `MAXBODY` (20 000 bytes) but the index records the real lengths.
- Two hosts with the same path no longer collide: the host is part of the name, and a `-2`/`-3` suffix is added if the same second produces the same host+path.
- Names carry no date (only `HHMMSS`), so **never sort flows by name across days** — `session`, `replay` and `snap` sort by mtime.

## The index [#the-index]

```bash
tail -3 /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl
```

```json
{"ts": 1795530833, "file": "200353_example_com__.txt", "host": "example.com", "method": "GET", "path": "/s.js", "status": 200, "req_len": 0, "resp_len": 1379}
```

Quick analysis:

```bash
# API surface, most frequent first
jq -r '"\(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sed 's/[0-9a-f]\{8,\}/<id>/g' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30

# errors only
jq -r 'select(.status >= 400) | "\(.status) \(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# what got sent where with a body
jq -r 'select(.req_len > 0) | "\(.req_len) \(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sort -rn | head
```

## Replay [#replay]

`replay` re-issues a captured request from the host, defaulting to *exactly* what the app sent, with explicit overrides:

```bash
replay --grep 'auth/session'                      # newest match
replay --grep 'auth/session' --session            # inject harvested cookie
replay --grep 'auth/session' --dry                # print, do not send
replay --grep 'chat/messages' --patch 'conversationId="<other>"'   # IDOR probe
replay --grep X --remove-header authorization --dry
replay --grep X -x                                # through mitmproxy → new flow
```

Patch syntax is a small JSONPath: `a.b`, `items[0].id`, `a.b[2].c`. Values are parsed as JSON when possible (`42`, `true`, `"str"`), else kept as strings.

Every `--patch` run should start with `--dry`. It prints the method, URL, headers and the first 300 bytes of body — enough to catch a typo before you send something destructive to a production backend.

## Why this beats Burp here [#why-this-beats-burp-here]

- **Same headers** as the app, including device-specific ones and the cookie jar state at capture time.
- **Attestation-friendly**: capture the login once, replay everything else; you never need a fresh keystore challenge for non-login endpoints.
- **Evidence-friendly**: `-x` re-sends through mitmproxy, so the attempt lands in the same flow corpus with a timestamp.

## Token harvesting [#token-harvesting]

`session` merges the WebView's `document.cookie`, `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` with the newest captured `Cookie` header (httpOnly cookies are invisible to JS):

```bash
session              # writes ~/.mobsec/session/<ts>.json and latest.json
session show
replay --grep 'chat/loadInitialData' --session
```

Storage layout:

```json
{"cdp": {"url": "…", "cookie": "…", "localStorage": {…}, "sessionStorage": {…}},
 "flow": {"file": "…", "cookie": "…"}}
```

## Spotting the interesting things [#spotting-the-interesting-things]

Patterns worth grepping for in a fresh corpus:

```bash
grep -rlE '"(role|isAdmin|permissions)"' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head
grep -rl 'secret\|token\|otp\|mfa' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head
grep -rhoE '"https?://[^"]+"' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | sort -u | head -40      # third-party surface
grep -rh 'set-cookie' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | sort -u | head                  # flags: HttpOnly? Secure? SameSite?
```

And the classic: compare what a **low-privilege** account gets versus a **high-privilege** one for the same endpoint — same request, two cookies, diff the bodies.

# Frida & instrumentation (/docs/frida)

Frida is not "installed" here, it is **wired**: the agent autostarts as a Magisk module under a different name, listens on loopback only, and the host side is a set of script profiles that answer specific questions.

## The device side [#the-device-side]

| Piece | Path |
|---|---|
| Binary | `/data/adb/fsrv/hluda` (renamed `frida-server`, 17.27.5, x86_64) |
| Config | `/data/adb/fsrv/conf` → `AUTOSTART=1`, `LISTEN=127.0.0.1:27042` |
| Control | `/data/adb/fsrv/ctl start\|stop\|status` |
| Module | `/data/adb/modules/fsrv` (starts it from `service.sh`) |

```bash
adb shell su -c '/data/adb/fsrv/ctl status'     # running pid=2180 listen=127.0.0.1:27042
frida-ps -U | head
```

Renaming matters: the string `frida-server` and the default port `27042` are what most detectors grep for in `/proc/net/tcp`, process lists and file paths. `hluda` is what a heavily-used public build calls itself; on loopback it is also invisible to the LAN.

## The host side [#the-host-side]

`frida` + `frida-tools` 17.27.5 (pipx), `objection` available for quick jobs, and these wrappers:

```bash
fspawn <pkg> [profile] [frida args…]   # force-stop, spawn under frida with a script set
fdp [pkg] [port]                       # discover webview_devtools_remote_<pid>, adb forward
cdp url | eval "<js>" | watch [secs]   # Chrome DevTools Protocol client for the WebView
session                                # harvest cookies/localStorage/sessionStorage
```

### Profiles [#profiles]

| Profile | Scripts | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `trace` | core, webview-debug, rootcheck, tls | first look: what does this app touch, what does it check |
| `web` | core, webview-debug | WebView/Tauri/Cordova apps — enables CDP |
| `attest` | core, keystore | key generation, attestation challenge, chain dump |
| `spy` | core, webview-debug + 3 Medusa modules | anti-root bypass, OkHttp logging, SQLite queries |
| `intercept` | 9 HTTP Toolkit scripts | pinning bypass + proxy override + CA injection + root-detect off |
| `full` | everything local | kitchen sink; expect noise |
| `raw` | none | isolate whether a script is the problem |

### The local script set [#the-local-script-set]

| File | What it hooks |
|---|---|
| `00-core.js` | logging helpers on `globalThis`, process/arch info, a **filtered** exception handler (only reports faults in app-owned libs, capped at 5 — Frida 17 removed `global`; use `globalThis`) |
| `05-webview-debug.js` | `WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)`, console messages, URL loads |
| `10-jni.js` | scans loaded classes for `tauri`/`plugin` classes, wraps methods, lists `libapp_lib.so` symbols matching `permanent_login|attest|secure_storage|plugin` |
| `20-keystore.js` | `KeyGenParameterSpec.setAttestationChallenge` / `setIsStrongBoxBacked`, `KeyStore.getCertificateChain` subject/issuer dump |
| `30-rootcheck.js` | `File.exists/canRead/canExecute/isFile/isDirectory` on su/magisk/frida/xposed paths, `Runtime.exec`, `getPackageInfo`, `Debug.isDebuggerConnected`, `Build` fields |
| `40-tls.js` | `SSLContext.init` trust managers, `NetworkSecurityPolicy`; `--bypass` = trust-all |

```bash
# with extra args, everything after the profile is passed to frida
fspawn com.example.app trace --runtime=v8
fspawn com.example.app raw -l ~/my-script.js
```

## Background runs [#background-runs]

Frida's REPL needs a tty. `frida -U -f pkg < /dev/null` exits immediately, and `pkill -f 'frida -U -f pkg'` can kill the shell that issued it. Use a fifo:

```bash
mkfifo /tmp/f; sleep 900 > /tmp/f &
fspawn com.example.app intercept < /tmp/f > /tmp/frida.log 2>&1 &
tail -f /tmp/frida.log
```

## WebView = CDP [#webview--cdp]

For hybrid apps this is the highest-value tool in the rig: no hooks, full DOM, console, network view and storage.

```bash
fspawn com.example.app web
fdp com.example.app          # pid=9918 socket=webview_devtools_remote_9918 -> http://127.0.0.1:9222
cdp url                      # {"id":…, "url":"https://app.example.com/chat", "title":"App"}
cdp eval "JSON.stringify(Object.keys(localStorage))"
cdp eval "document.cookie"
cdp watch 15                 # stream console + network events for 15 s
```

`session` uses the same channel to merge `document.cookie`, `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` with the newest captured `cookie` header (httpOnly cookies never show up in JS).

## Stolen modules (Medusa) [#stolen-modules-medusa]

`tools/medusa` is a vendored copy; `bin/medusa-export` converts its JSON modules into standalone JS:

```bash
medusa-export list
medusa-export export --set core      # writes frida/medusa/*.js
medusa-export export http_communications__okhttp3_retrofit
```

Medusa's modules assume the framework's helpers (`colorLog`, `Module.findExportByName`). The exporter injects a shim: `Color`, `colorLog`, `Options` defaults, `__mod('libc.so', …)`, plus Frida-17 polyfills for `Module.findExportByName` / `getExportByName`.

<Callout type="error" title="`file_system__shared_preferences` crashes WebView apps">
It replaces `getSharedPreferences()` globally and Chromium then dies with
`NullPointerException: … SharedPreferences$Editor.apply() on a null object reference`.
Keep it out of profiles for any app with a WebView; load it by hand only for native-only apps.
</Callout>

## When Frida itself is the problem [#when-frida-itself-is-the-problem]

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Failed to spawn: unable to find process` | package not installed / wrong user | `adb shell pm list packages \| grep name` |
| spawns then instantly detaches | script threw at load | run profile `raw`, then add scripts one by one |
| `access-violation` spam | the exception handler reporting ART's own SIGSEGVs | already filtered in `00-core.js`; check the PC is in an app lib |
| `frida-ps` hangs | server died (OOM, or killed by a detector) | `/data/adb/fsrv/ctl start` |

# Glossary (/docs/glossary)

**adb reverse** — forwards a port on the *device* to the host. Used so the app can reach mitmproxy on `127.0.0.1:18080` without a LAN proxy. Dies on every reboot.

**Attestation chain** — certificate chain returned by the Android keystore for a generated key: leaf (app key) → TEE intermediate → Droid CA → Google root. Encodes device identity, lock state and verified-boot status.

**AVD** — Android Virtual Device. Here: `pentest16`, pixel_7 profile, API 36 Play Store image.

**Bootloader locked / verified boot** — properties the server can read from the attestation extension. TrickyStore's keybox decides what the server sees.

**CDP** — Chrome DevTools Protocol. Over `adb forward :9222` it gives DOM, console, storage and network for any debuggable WebView.

**Cert-Fixer** — Magisk module that bind-mounts user CAs into `/apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts` at `post-fs-data`, so system apps (GMS, Play Store) trust mitmproxy.

**conscrypt** — Android's TLS provider and the place the system trust store lives since Android 14 (moved out of `/system/etc/security/cacerts`).

**denylist (Magisk)** — packages that get *no* module injection. Empty in this rig on purpose: TrickyStore/PIF must reach the target app.

**denylist policy (Zygisk Next)** — `default` (inject everywhere except denylisted) or `whitelist` (inject only listed). Whitelist breaks WebView renderer sandboxes.

**frida-server** — the on-device agent. Here renamed `hluda`, autostarted by the `fsrv` Magisk module, listening on loopback only.

**gadget** — Frida's injectable library for non-rooted devices; requires patching and re-signing the APK, which changes its signature. Not used here.

**HMA-OSS** — "Hide My Applist" fork: hides installed packages from a target app's enumeration. Installed, hide list empty.

**keybox.xml** — TrickyStore's replacement cert+key material: EC and/or RSA chains plus private keys. Must be hardware (RKP), unexpired and unrevoked.

**keybox revocation list** — Google's published serial blacklist at `android.googleapis.com/attestation/status`. Server-side check; cannot be spoofed locally.

**KVM** — kernel virtual machine; `/dev/kvm` + `kvm` group membership makes the emulator usable.

**Magisk** — systemless root. Version 31.1 here, applied to the system image's ramdisk via rootAVD.

**mitmproxy / mitmdump** — the intercepting proxy. `mitm/dump.py` addon writes one file per flow.

**Play Integrity (PI)** — Google's app-level integrity API (device/app/account verdicts). Emulator → `NO_INTEGRITY`; not solvable here.

**PIF (PlayIntegrityFix)** — module that tries to satisfy PI by spoofing props; on an emulator it still fails.

**post-fs-data** — earliest Magisk boot stage; where Cert-Fixer mounts CAs.

**RKP** — Remote Key Provisioning. Modern hardware attestation where keys/certs are provisioned by Google per device.

**rootAVD** — script that patches an AVD's `ramdisk.img` with Magisk; modifies the system image, not the AVD config.

**snapshot (AVD)** — full VM state save/restore (`adb emu avd snapshot save`). ~5 GB, ~25 s restore.

**TrickyStore** — Zygisk module that substitutes keystore attestation chains for packages in `target.txt` using `keybox.xml`.

**TEE** — Trusted Execution Environment; hardware side that produces attestation. Emulators fake it (`teeBroken=true`).

**Zygisk** — Magisk's code-injection mechanism into zygote-spawned apps. Disabled in Magisk itself here; **Zygisk Next** provides it.

**zygiskd** — Zygisk Next's control CLI (`status`, `enforce-denylist`, `denylist-policy`, `memory-type`).

**`Zygisk-Assistant`** — popular root-hiding module. Not used: it requires targets in Magisk's denylist, which strips our spoofing modules from those same apps.

# mobsec — an Android pentest rig that actually works (/docs)

A rooted Android 16 emulator on this laptop, wired end to end: **HTTPS decrypted**, **Frida attached from the first instruction**, **root hidden**, and **hardware-backed key attestation spoofed** well enough that a real bank-grade server accepts the login.

Everything here runs locally. No cloud, no extra hardware, ~20 GB of disk.

<Callout type="warn" title="Authorised testing only">
The attestation layer makes this device claim to be a different physical phone, and the keybox in use is not ours. Use it against apps you are permitted to test. Nothing in this rig is anonymous: traffic goes out from your own IP.
</Callout>

## What you get [#what-you-get]

| Capability | How | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Android 16 x86_64 emulator, Play Store image | `pentest16` AVD (pixel_7, 6 GB RAM, 16 GB data) | [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart) |
| Root + Magisk modules | rootAVD + Magisk 31.1, Zygisk Next, TrickyStore, PIF 4.9, Cert-Fixer | [Architecture](/docs/architecture) |
| HTTPS interception for *every* app | mitmproxy + system CA bind-mounted into `conscrypt` | [Interception](/docs/interception) |
| Certificate pinning bypass | HTTP Toolkit script set via `fspawn … intercept` | [Interception](/docs/interception#pinning) |
| Frida, ready in one command | `frida-server` as a Magisk module + script profiles | [Frida](/docs/frida) |
| WebView DOM, console, storage access | Chrome DevTools Protocol over `adb forward` | [Frida](/docs/frida#webview) |
| Capture → edit → replay any request | `nettap` + `replay` harness | [Flows](/docs/flows) |
| Hardware key attestation spoofing | TrickyStore + a valid RKP keybox | [Attestation](/docs/attestation) |
| Root/emulator hiding | Zygisk denylist policy, anonymous memory, HMA-OSS scoped per target | [Root hiding](/docs/stealth) |

| A checklist that maps to these commands | HackTricks/MASTG in rig terms | [Pentest checklist](/docs/checklist) |
| Static APK recon in one command | `recon` (apkid + apkleaks + mobsfscan + jadx) | [Static recon](/docs/recon) |
| Instant return to a logged-in state | AVD snapshots | [Snapshots](/docs/snapshots) |

## 30-second health check [#30-second-health-check]

```bash
pentestctl status
```

```text
device        ok   emulator-5554  sdk_gphone64_x86_64  android 16 sdk 36
root          ok   uid=0(root) ... context=u:r:magisk:s0
zygisk        ok   inject_state=1  denylist_policy=0  enforce=1  memory=1
attestation   --   keybox DeviceID="RKP keybox. Join my group: …" (cosmetic)   ok   leaf valid until 2026-12-04 (8d left)
frida         ok   frida-server running pid=2180 listen=127.0.0.1:27042
interception  ok   mitmdump up   adb reverse ok   proxy 127.0.0.1:18080
```

If something is red, `pentestctl fix` repairs the two things that break on every reboot (`adb reverse` and the mitm addon), then see [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting).

## The one-paragraph mental model [#the-one-paragraph-mental-model]

The emulator boots a **Magisk-patched ramdisk**, so `su` works from the first second. Magisk loads three Zygisk modules that matter: **TrickyStore** fakes the hardware keystore's attestation chain for packages listed in `target.txt`, **PlayIntegrityFix** tries (and fails, on an emulator) to satisfy Play Integrity, and **Zygisk Next** does the injecting in anonymous memory. **Cert-Fixer** bind-mounts our mitmproxy CA into every process's trust store, including system ones. **frida-server** runs renamed as `hluda` under a small custom module, listening on loopback only. On the host, `nettap` keeps mitmproxy and the `adb reverse` tunnel alive, `fspawn` starts an app under Frida with a chosen script profile, and `replay` re-issues anything you captured.

## Where things live [#where-things-live]

```text
~/mobsec/                  the rig (this repo of scripts + docs)
├── bin/                   pentestctl, nettap, fspawn, fdp, cdp, session, replay, recon,
│                        entry, pull-data, integrity, hma, keybox-refresh, docs, snap, uitap, asu
├── frida/                 instrumentation scripts (+ httptoolkit/, medusa/)
├── mitm/                  dump.py addon (flow capture)
├── modules/               Magisk module zips
├── tools/                 frida-server, jadx, apktool, kbcheck.py, keybox roots
├── docs/                  this site
└── build/                 fsrv module (frida autostart)

~/Android/Sdk/             Android SDK (patched system image lives here)
~/.android/avd/pentest16*  the emulator
/tmp/mtflows/              captured flows (txt + _index.jsonl)
~/.mobsec/session/         harvested cookies/tokens
~/.mobsec/recon/           static analysis reports
```

## Start reading here [#start-reading-here]

1. [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart) — a device that is already built, or build it from zero.
2. [Daily workflow](/docs/workflow) — the loop you will actually repeat.
3. [Architecture](/docs/architecture) — why each layer exists, and what breaks without it.

# Play Integrity (the other attestation) (/docs/integrity)

Two different things get called "attestation" in Android pentests, and confusing them wastes days:

| | What it proves | Who checks it | Can this rig fake it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Key attestation** (Android Keystore / RKP) | "this key lives in a TEE on a device whose boot state is X" | your target's backend, per-request | **Yes** — TrickyStore + keybox, see [Attestation](/docs/attestation) |
| **Play Integrity** (`IntegrityManager.requestIntegrityToken`) | "this APK, installed from Play, on a Google-approved device, right now" | Google evaluates, your backend reads the verdict JSON | **No**, not on an emulator |

Play Integrity is Google's own server-side verdict. You cannot compute it locally, and the request only works for a Play-distributed, Play-signed app with a Play Console project — which is why pentest tooling ships its own checker APK.

## Measuring it on this rig [#measuring-it-on-this-rig]

```bash
integrity          # taps the button in SPIC, scrapes the verdict JSON from logcat
integrity --json          # raw verdict
```

`integrity` drives **SPIC** (`com.henrikherzig.playintegritychecker`, in `apks/`): force-stops it, launches it, finds the "Make Play Integrity Request" button via `uiautomator dump`, taps it, and parses the JSON block SPIC prints to `I/System.out` (that is where the library dumps the token payload).

Measured on this AVD, twice, before and after PlayIntegrityFix:

```text
package           : com.henrikherzig.playintegritychecker
app recognition   : UNEVALUATED
device verdict    : —
recent activity   : UNEVALUATED
app licensing     : UNEVALUATED
play protect      : UNEVALUATED
```

`UNEVALUATED` (and a *missing* `deviceRecognitionVerdict`) is not an error in the rig. Logcat shows the request itself succeeding:

```text
I/Finsky: Integrity key attestation record generated successfully
I/Integrity: requestIntegrityToken() finished for com.henrikherzig.playintegritychecker
```

Google receives the request and declines to grade it: the device is an emulator and **no Google account is signed in**. Both conditions must be satisfied for a verdict to exist at all — and even with an account, a Play Store emulator image still cannot return `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY`.

<Callout type="info" title="Creating a Google account on the AVD is not worth it">
It removes the `UNEVALUATED` state and replaces it with a clean `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY` / no `DEVICE` result. It does not unlock anything, and it puts a real account on a rooted emulator.
</Callout>

## The modules, and why they do not help here [#the-modules-and-why-they-do-not-help-here]

- **PlayIntegrityFix 4.9** (`playintegrityfix`) patches device props in GMS's process so DroidGuard is less likely to notice the emulator. It is installed and loading (`zygiskd status` lists it) — it just cannot manufacture a device verdict that Google refuses to issue.
- **PlayIntegrityFork v19** is parked in `modules/archive/`: it ships **only** `arm64-v8a` and `armeabi-v7a` Zygisk libs, so on this x86_64 image it silently never loads. Watch for that class of bug with `zygiskd status` after every module change — the module staying absent from `modules64:` is the tell.
- **TrickyStore** fakes the keystore chain. Play Integrity's `STRONG_INTEGRITY` needs a hardware-backed signature over the *app signing key* by a Google-trusted root — key attestation spoofing gets you partway, then Google's own evaluation of the resulting record is the wall.
- **TEESimulator** (JingMatrix, GPL-3.0) is the current community answer: a software KeyMint that needs a keybox, designed for exactly this "make a non-device look like a device" problem. It is a candidate upgrade for this rig; it is not installed, and it would still be fighting Play's verdict rather than key attestation.

## When your target actually gates on Play Integrity [#when-your-target-actually-gates-on-play-integrity]

In order of cost:

1. **Check it is really PI.** If the app also sends a key-attestation chain (Tauri/Rust/native apps often do), the keybox path already covers you — Target is exactly this case.
2. **Frida-hook the client side.** `IntegrityManager.requestIntegrityToken` / the verdict parser in the app: hook the callback and hand back a verdict the app likes. Works only when the backend trusts the *client* to inspect the verdict, which is a bug worth reporting in itself.
3. **Replay with a good token.** `session` + `replay` let you re-issue the request with a token minted on a clean device — that is the same thing a real attacker does, and it demonstrates the missing server-side binding.
4. **Use a physical device.** No emulator configuration passes `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY`; that is the point of the product.

## Related traps [#related-traps]

<Callout type="warn" title="`integrity` needs the screen awake and unlocked">
`uiautomator dump` returns nothing useful on a locked screen, and the tap lands nowhere. `adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_WAKEUP` first if the AVD has been idle.
</Callout>

<Callout type="warn" title="SPIC's JSON block ends at an *unindented* `}`">
The verdict is a multi-line pretty-printed document in logcat. Closing braces of nested objects are indented; only the final one is flush left. Any scraper that stops at the first `}` truncates the JSON and reports "no verdict" — a bug that cost an hour here.
</Callout>

# HTTPS interception (/docs/interception)

The goal is boring reliability: every app on the device, including Play Store and GMS, decrypts through mitmproxy, and apps that pin certificates still connect.

## The chain [#the-chain]

<Mermaid chart="flowchart LR\n  A[app] -->|CONNECT :18080| B[adb reverse tunnel]\n  B --> C[mitmdump :18080<br/>mitm/dump.py]\n  C --> D[upstream]\n  C -->|mitmproxy CA| A\n  E[Cert-Fixer<br/>post-fs-data] -.->|bind-mount CA| F[/apex/…/conscrypt/cacerts/]\n  F -.->|trust store| A" />

1. **`adb reverse tcp:18080 tcp:18080`** — device port 18080 is the host's mitmdump. Survives nothing; re-established by `nettap on`.
2. **Global proxy** `127.0.0.1:18080` (optional once `fspawn intercept` is in play).
3. **CA trust** — the mitmproxy CA is installed as a *user* CA (`/data/misc/user/0/cacerts-added/<hash>.0`) and then mounted into the system trust store by **Cert-Fixer** at boot.
4. **Capture** — `mitm/dump.py` writes one file per interesting flow.

## The CA, exactly [#the-ca-exactly]

```bash
# hash used by the Android trust store (old subject hash, not the new one)
openssl x509 -inform PEM -subject_hash_old -in ~/.mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem | head -1
# c8750f0d
```

Installed at `/data/misc/user/0/cacerts-added/c8750f0d.0`; Cert-Fixer copies and bind-mounts it into `/apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts` for every process, and does the same inside PID 1's mount namespace so late-started system services inherit it.

Verify for a specific process:

```bash
PID=$(adb shell pidof com.google.android.gms | tr -d '\r')
adb shell su -c "nsenter --mount=/proc/$PID/ns/mnt -- ls /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts | wc -l"   # 150
adb shell su -c "nsenter --mount=/proc/$PID/ns/mnt -- ls /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts/c8750f0d.0"
```

<Callout type="info" title="Why AlwaysTrustUserCerts was not enough">
That module only mounts in `service.sh`, i.e. **after** GMS and Play Store have already started, so they kept their original trust store and failed with `Client TLS handshake failed … does not trust the proxy's certificate for play-fe.googleapis.com`. Cert-Fixer hooks `post-fs-data` instead. It is installed, `trustusercerts` is disabled via `touch /data/adb/modules/trustusercerts/disable`.
</Callout>

## Pinning [#pinning]

Two independent mechanisms, both from HTTP Toolkit's Frida scripts (`frida/httptoolkit/`), loaded by `fspawn <pkg> intercept`:

- **`android-certificate-unpinning.js`** — hooks `TrustManagerImpl`, `OkHttp CertificatePinner`, `X509TrustManager` wrappers, Conscrypt and a long list of third-party pinning libraries, and makes them accept anything.
- **`android-certificate-unpinning-fallback.js`** — a second pass that patches classes *after* they load, for apps that cache their trust managers early.

Plus two scripts that make interception work without a system proxy:

- **`android-proxy-override.js`** — rewrites `System.getProperty("http.proxyHost")`, `ConnectivityManager.getDefaultProxy()` and OkHttp's proxy selector.
- **`native-connect-hook.js` / `native-tls-hook.js`** — LD_PRELOAD-style hooks (`connect`, `getaddrinfo`, `SSL_*`) so native code (Rust/Flutter/Go) also goes through the proxy and trusts our CA.

Proof, reproducible on this device:

```bash
fspawn tech.httptoolkit.pinning_demo intercept
# tap "OkHTTP pinned request" → the app reports success, and the flow shows up:
# GET https://rsa8192--untrusted-root.testserver.host/ HTTP/2.0
```

Without the profile the same button says **Failed** and no flow appears.

## What still resists [#what-still-resists]

| Case | Symptom | Workaround |
|---|---|---|
| Certificate **transparency** enforcement | `SSL handshake failed` inside a pinned library, even with unpinning | Not solved here; needs a CT-aware proxy or hooking the CT verifier (`--ct` hooks in some forks) |
| Mutual TLS with a hardware key | login fails at the TLS layer | Keys live in TEE; only TrickyStore-style keystore spoofing can help, and only for attestation, not arbitrary mTLS |
| QUIC / HTTP/3 | app works, nothing captured | Disable QUIC in the app or block UDP 443 on the device; mitmproxy does not proxy QUIC |
| WebSocket over `wss` | decrypted once upgraded | mitmproxy captures the upgrade; use the addon's `websocket_message` hook if you need frames |
| Apps that pin inside a **WebView WebAssembly** module | nothing in Java hooks fires | hook the WebView's network stack (`fspawn web`) or fall back to `replay` with harvested tokens |

## The addon [#the-addon]

```bash
cat ~/mobsec/mitm/dump.py
```

- `FLOWDIR` (default `/tmp/mtflows`), `INTEREST` (only matching URLs), `IGNORE` (default drops googleapis/gstatic/ggbn/firebase/app-measurement/crashlytics noise), `MAXBODY` (20000 bytes per body).
- Output `<HHMMSS>_<host>_<path>.txt`, plus `_index.log` (human) and `_index.jsonl` (machine).
- Restart after editing: `nettap off && nettap on`. mitmproxy does **not** hot-reload addons.

## Sanity checks that catch most "interception is broken" reports [#sanity-checks-that-catch-most-interception-is-broken-reports]

```bash
pentestctl status | sed -n '/interception/,$p'
curl -s -x 127.0.0.1:18080 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.org   # 200
grep -c 'does not trust the proxy' /tmp/mitm.log                                   # want 0 for GMS
ls -t /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head -3
```

# Quickstart (/docs/quickstart)

Two paths: the device already exists (this laptop), or you are rebuilding it on a fresh machine.

## Path A — the device already exists [#path-a--the-device-already-exists]

```bash
# 1. health check (start the emulator first if it is not running)
~/Android/Sdk/emulator/emulator -avd pentest16 -no-snapshot -no-boot-anim &
pentestctl status

# 2. repair the two things a reboot always breaks
pentestctl fix

# 3. capture traffic
nettap on
# ... use the app ...
ls -t /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head

# 4. instrument the app (Frida + pinning bypass + CA injection)
fspawn com.example.app intercept

# 5. WebView console/DOM/storage
fdp com.example.app      # forwards :9222, prints the DevTools target
cdp url                  # what page is loaded
cdp eval "document.title"
```

<Callout type="idea" title="Fastest possible daily start">
```bash
snap load logged-in      # ~25 s instead of ~90 s cold boot
pentestctl fix
```
`snap load` restores apps, sessions and cookies exactly as you left them. See [Snapshots](/docs/snapshots).
</Callout>

## Path B — rebuild from zero [#path-b--rebuild-from-zero]

The full beginner walkthrough (SDK install, AVD tuning, rootAVD/Magisk UI clicks, module URLs, CA install, verification) lives in `GUIDE-from-scratch.md` in the repo root (open it directly, it is not part of this site). Short version:

```bash
cd ~/mobsec
./bootstrap.sh --sdk        # host deps + SDK + AVD  (needs your sudo password once, for udev)
emulator -avd pentest16 -no-snapshot &
./fetch-deps.sh             # frida-server, jadx, apktool, scrcpy, rootAVD
./rootAVD.sh …              # see GUIDE step 4 — interactive, Magisk UI driven over adb
./install-device.sh         # modules, frida-server, zygisk policy
./setup-keybox.sh           # fetch + validate a keybox, install to TrickyStore
./setup-net.sh              # CA into the system store, proxy + tunnel
pentestctl status
```

Order matters: `install-device.sh` reboots the device, `setup-net.sh` must run **after** the first boot with modules installed, and `setup-keybox.sh` last (it validates against the live device's TrickyStore path).

<Callout type="warn" title="One interactive step cannot be scripted">
Magisk's "install → patch image → additional setup → reboot" flow is UI-driven. `rootAVD.sh` pauses for it; the `GUIDE-from-scratch.md` section 4 walks the exact taps, and `uitap` can drive most of them by text.
</Callout>

## First real verification (5 minutes) [#first-real-verification-5-minutes]

Do not trust a green `pentestctl status` alone — prove each layer with a request:

| Layer | Command | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| Interception | `curl -s -x 127.0.0.1:18080 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://example.org` | `200`, plus a new flow file |
| System trust (GMS) | open Play Store, check `/tmp/mitm.log` | no `does not trust the proxy's certificate` |
| Pinning bypass | `fspawn tech.httptoolkit.pinning_demo intercept` → tap "OkHTTP pinned request" | label says **Success**, request appears in flows |
| Frida | `fspawn com.android.settings web` | `[fspawn] … scripts=2`, no exception spam |
| WebView CDP | `fdp && cdp url` | the app's page URL |
| Attestation | `KeyAttestation` app → "Attest key" | leaf issuer `O=TEE,CN=<deviceid>`, "Bootloader is locked" |

## Sharing this site [#sharing-this-site]

The site is served by MkDocs on the host. By default it listens on loopback only:

```bash
docs serve                 # http://127.0.0.1:8000/
docs serve --lan           # http://<this-host-ip>:8000/ — phone, second laptop, whatever
docs status                # what it is bound to, and every URL that answers
```

Two things have to be true for another device to load it:

1. **It is bound to `0.0.0.0`**, not `127.0.0.1` (`docs serve --lan` does that; `docs status` shows the bind).
2. **The host firewall lets the port in.** On a box with `ufw` enabled the default inbound policy is
   `DROP`, so once:

   ```bash
   sudo ufw allow 8000/tcp
   # narrower: sudo ufw allow from 192.168.0.0/24 to any port 8000 proto tcp
   ```

To keep it up permanently (survives logout/reboot, restarts on failure):

```bash
systemctl --user enable --now mobsec-docs        # unit in ~/.config/systemd/user/
journalctl --user -u mobsec-docs -f
```

It is a plain MkDocs site: no auth, no TLS. Anyone on that network can read the whole rig, including
which target you are testing — put it behind Tailscale or an SSH tunnel
(`ssh -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 host`) if the network is not yours.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

- [Daily workflow](/docs/workflow) — the loop on a real engagement.
- [Interception](/docs/interception) — why pinning bypass works, and what still fails.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) — the eight traps, in the order they usually hit.

# Rebuild from scratch (/docs/rebuild)

Two artefacts describe a rebuild:

- **`GUIDE-from-scratch.md`** — the narrative walkthrough (12 sections, beginner-friendly, includes the interactive Magisk UI steps and every download URL).
- **`bootstrap.sh` / `fetch-deps.sh` / `install-device.sh` / `setup-keybox.sh` / `setup-net.sh`** — the automated path, in that order.

## Automated path [#automated-path]

```bash
git clone <your copy> ~/mobsec && cd ~/mobsec

./bootstrap.sh --sdk        # host deps, pipx tools, Android SDK, AVD creation, PATH block
emulator -avd pentest16 -no-snapshot -no-boot-anim &
./fetch-deps.sh             # frida-server (x86_64 + arm64), jadx, apktool, scrcpy, rootAVD
# >>> root the image with rootAVD (interactive, see GUIDE §4) <<<
./install-device.sh         # Magisk modules, frida-server staging, zygisk policy, reboot
./setup-keybox.sh           # fetch + validate + install a keybox
./setup-net.sh              # install mitm CA into the system store, proxy + tunnel
pentestctl status
```

### Why the order is fixed [#why-the-order-is-fixed]

| Step | Depends on | Fails if skipped |
|---|---|---|
| `bootstrap.sh` | — | no SDK/adb/emulator/AVD |
| `fetch-deps.sh` | network | nothing to install downstream |
| rootAVD | booted, unrooted device | `install-device.sh` aborts on missing `su` |
| `install-device.sh` | root | no TrickyStore/PIF/Cert-Fixer/fsrv |
| `setup-keybox.sh` | TrickyStore on device | attestation stays software/AOSP |
| `setup-net.sh` | Cert-Fixer installed + one boot | user apps work, GMS/Play Store do not |

`install-device.sh` finishes with a reboot; wait for `adb wait-for-device` before continuing.

### What is interactive [#what-is-interactive]

Only Magisk's first-run flow: *Install → Patch firmware/image → Select from storage → fakeboot.img → OK → additional setup → reboot*, plus granting `su` to shell. `GUIDE §4` has the exact taps; `uitap` can drive them by text, but expect to babysit it once.

## Sharing the rig with a colleague [#sharing-the-rig-with-a-colleague]

```bash
zip -qr ~/share-zip/mobsec-rig-$(date +%Y%m%d).zip ~/mobsec \
  -x '*/tools/jadx*' '*/tools/scrcpy*' '*/tools/apktool*' '*/tools/frida-server-*' \
     '*/modules/MagiskFrida*' '*/modules/archive/*' '*/apks/*' '*/tools/medusa/.venv/*' \
     '*/site/*' '*/.mobsec/*' '*/__pycache__/*'
```

Deliberately excluded, with reasons:

| Excluded | Why |
|---|---|
| `keybox.xml`, `.pem`, `.p12` | key material; the recipient must fetch their own |
| `~/.mobsec/session`, `~/.mitmproxy` | live cookies/tokens and your private CA |
| AVD snapshots | 5 GB each, host-specific |
| tool binaries (jadx, scrcpy, frida-server) | re-downloadable via `fetch-deps.sh`, keeps the zip ~25 MB |
| `MagiskFrida-*.zip` | 141 MB, superseded by the `fsrv` module |

The recipient still needs **their own** `adb` device and must run `setup-net.sh` so their mitmproxy CA (not ours) is installed. `SHARING.md` in the archive carries the exact run order and this table.

## Verification after a rebuild [#verification-after-a-rebuild]

```bash
pentestctl status                                  # every section green
frida-ps -U | head -3                              # 150+ processes
curl -s -x 127.0.0.1:18080 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.org   # 200
fspawn tech.httptoolkit.pinning_demo intercept     # "OkHTTP pinned request - Success"
recon com.android.settings --deep                  # recon sanity check
snap save logged-in                                # your first restore point
```

## Version pinning that matters [#version-pinning-that-matters]

| Component | Version | Why pinned |
|---|---|---|
| Magisk | 31.1 | Zygisk Next expects it; older Magisk has no `--sqlite` settings write |
| Zygisk Next | 1.5.3-880 | later builds changed `zygiskd` flags |
| frida-server | 17.27.5 | must match host `frida` exactly; 17.x removed `global`, changed `Module` API |
| Frida host | 17.27.5 | mismatch = "unable to communicate with remote frida-server" |
| PlayIntegrityFix | 4.9-inject-s | v19 has no x86_64 zygisk lib |
| jadx | 1.5.7 | apkleaks shells out to it |
| mitmproxy | 12.3.1 | addon uses `http.HTTPFlow` API (stable since 9) |

When you bump a version, re-run the [verification list](#verification-after-a-rebuild) top to bottom before trusting the rig.

# Static recon (/docs/recon)

Dynamic testing tells you what the app *did*; static testing tells you what it *can* do. `recon` runs the static pass in one command and produces a report you can read in two minutes.

## Usage [#usage]

```bash
recon /path/to/app.apk
recon com.example.app --deep        # pulls base.apk from the device, then decompiles
recon app.apk -o /tmp/out
```

Output:

```text
~/.mobsec/recon/<pkg>-<timestamp>/
├── report.md            <- read this
├── app.apk
└── raw/
    ├── badging.txt      aapt2 dump badging
    ├── manifest.xml     apkanalyzer manifest print
    ├── apkid.txt        packers / obfuscators / anti-analysis
    ├── apkleaks.json    secrets + endpoints (+ .log)
    ├── mobsfscan.json   SAST rules
    └── endpoints.txt    only with --deep (jadx + grep)
```

## What the report contains, and how to read it [#what-the-report-contains-and-how-to-read-it]

### Exported components [#exported-components]
The attack surface that does not require the app to be running. For each component: `permission`, `actions`, `categories`, `data` (scheme/host/path/mime). Anything exported without a signature-level permission is worth a `adb shell am start` / `am broadcast` probe.

### Packers / anti-analysis (APKiD) [#packers--anti-analysis-apkid]
Read this with suspicion. APKiD matches library code too:

| Tag | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `packer: …` | packer/obfuscator heuristic | decide whether to test the packed layer or the loader |
| `anti_vm` / `anti_debug` | emulator/debugger checks | **verify by reading the class** before believing it |
| `compiler: unknown` | not a real finding | ignore |

Concrete example from this rig: Target was tagged `anti_vm` + `packer: DexGuard`, and every hit turned out to be library code:

- `W0/c.java` → Firebase CCT metadata (`sdk-version`, `Build.MODEL`, `Build.FINGERPRINT`)
- `p003a2/v.java` → Material `MaterialAutoCompleteTextView` (a Meizu hint workaround)
- `p045n1/k.java` → GMS `DialogRedirect` logging
- `p019g/A.java` → `!"robolectric".equals(Build.FINGERPRINT)`

So: no app-level emulator check in the DEX. The `DexGuard` tag was R8 single-letter-package confusion. Ten minutes of reading beat a day of chasing a phantom.

### Secrets / endpoints (apkleaks) [#secrets--endpoints-apkleaks]
Categories with hit counts. Triage rules:

- `Google_API_Key` / `Firebase` keys are **usually not secrets** — they are restricted by package name + SHA-1. Report only if a restriction test shows otherwise.
- Random 30–40 char strings tagged `Artifactory_Password` are frequently obfuscation noise; grep the decompiled tree for the value before writing a finding.
- Version strings (`1.0.0.2`) match `IP_Address`; ignore.
- Real finds look like: hardcoded bearer tokens, private endpoints, staging hosts, cloud storage buckets.

### SAST (mobsfscan) [#sast-mobsfscan]
Rule-based Android checks (exported components, weak crypto, WebView settings, backup flags…). Fast, noisy, useful as a checklist. Zero findings is a valid result — not proof of safety.

### Deep mode [#deep-mode]
`--deep` decompiles with jadx (1.5.7) and greps string literals for URLs, then writes `endpoints.txt`. Use it to build the API list before you even launch the app; combine with the captured flows later.

## A realistic order of operations [#a-realistic-order-of-operations]

1. `recon com.example.app --deep` — components, permissions, endpoints, secrets.
2. Note the **exported** components and any endpoint that looks internal (`/admin`, `/internal`, versioned staging hosts).
3. Launch with `fspawn com.example.app web` (or `intercept`) and capture the real request set.
4. Diff static endpoints vs captured endpoints: what the app *can* call but did not is where the interesting bugs live.
5. Only then start `replay` fuzzing.

## Extending it [#extending-it]

`recon` is a shell script; every step is independent (`aapt2`, `apkanalyzer`, `apkid`, `apkleaks`, `mobsfscan`, `jadx`). Add steps by copying the pattern in `~/mobsec/bin/recon` — each writes into `raw/` and appends a section to `report.md`.

Useful manual follow-ups it does not do:

```bash
# who signs it / is it debuggable
apksigner verify --print-certs app.apk
aapt2 dump xmltree app.apk --file AndroidManifest.xml | grep -i debuggable

# backend fingerprinting from the flows
jq -r 'select(.status>=400) | "\(.status) \(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
```

# Snapshots (/docs/snapshots)

A cold boot costs ~90 seconds plus a login. A snapshot restore costs ~25 seconds and comes back to whatever state was saved — **including a logged-in app, if that is what you froze**.

## Commands [#commands]

```bash
snap list                 # name, size, timestamp of newest file
snap save                 # save as 'logged-in' (default)
snap save before-fuzz     # named
snap load                 # restore 'logged-in'
snap load before-fuzz
snap rm before-fuzz
snap boot                 # cold boot, no snapshot
```

Under the hood:

```bash
adb emu avd snapshot save logged-in
emulator -avd pentest16 -snapshot logged-in -no-snapshot-save -no-boot-anim
```

`-no-snapshot-save` is deliberate: when the emulator exits it would otherwise overwrite the snapshot with whatever half-broken state you were in.

## What survives a restore [#what-survives-a-restore]

| Survives | Does not survive |
|---|---|
| installed apps and their data | `adb reverse` tunnel (host-side) |
| logged-in sessions/cookies in app storage | mitmdump process (host-side) |
| Magisk modules + mount state | sometimes frida-server (`pentestctl fix` restarts it) |
| keybox, target.txt | global proxy setting? (survives, but points at a dead tunnel) |

That is why the documented restore sequence is:

```bash
snap load logged-in
pentestctl fix          # re-establishes reverse + frida
pentestctl status
```

## When a snapshot is a trap [#when-a-snapshot-is-a-trap]

Snapshots capture **mount state**, so a snapshot taken while a module was broken keeps restoring the broken mount. Symptoms: Cert-Fixer log says it ran, but GMS still cannot TLS. Fix: cold boot (`snap boot`), verify, then `snap save` again under a new name.

Rules:

- After installing/removing a Magisk module or changing the CA, **cold boot once**, verify `pentestctl status` + a GMS request, then save a new snapshot.
- Keep at most a handful: each is ~5 GB.
- Name by intent (`logged-in`, `pre-fuzz`, `clean-no-modules`), not by date.
- **A snapshot is only as logged-in as the moment you saved it.** After `keybox-refresh` rotates the
  keybox, the device presents a new attestation identity on the next launch and the backend drops the
  session — a snapshot saved before the rotation restores a logged-out app. Re-login (you need the
  TOTP), then `snap save logged-in` again.

<Callout type="warn" title="`snap save` refuses to work after `snap load`">
`load`/`boot` start the emulator with `-no-snapshot-save` so a broken session cannot overwrite a
good snapshot. The emulator reports the refusal as `UNSUPPORTED_VK_APP`, which looks like a GPU
problem and is not. `snap save <name> --reopen` cold-boots keeping `/data`, then saves.
</Callout>

## Cost [#cost]

| Action | Time | Disk |
|---|---|---|
| cold boot | ~90 s | — |
| snapshot restore | ~21–25 s | — |
| one snapshot | — | ~5.2 GB |
